```{r}
#| include: false
force_eval <- identical(Sys.getenv("DSPRRR_VIGNETTES_EVAL"), "true") ||
  identical(Sys.getenv("VITALS_SHOULD_EVAL"), "true")
in_check <- !force_eval && (
  nzchar(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_")) ||
  identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "false")
)

has_pins <- requireNamespace("pins", quietly = TRUE)
should_eval <- !in_check &&
  requireNamespace("vcr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  dsprrr:::eval_vignette()

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = should_eval
)

if (should_eval) {
  if (!is.null(vcr::current_cassette())) {
    try(vcr::eject_cassette(), silent = TRUE)
  }
  vcr::vcr_configure(
    dir = "_vcr",
    filter_request_headers = c("Authorization", "x-api-key"),
    match_requests_on = c("method", "uri")
  )
  vcr::setup_knitr()
}
```

Compiling a module produces demos, instructions, and tuned settings that you do
not want to recompute every time R restarts. This tutorial shows how to save a
compiled module to disk with `save_program()`, share versioned copies on a
[pins](https://pins.rstudio.com) board, restore it cleanly in a new session,
and inspect the traces it records as it runs.

```{r setup}
#| eval: true
#| message: false
library(dsprrr)
library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_openai(model = "gpt-6-luna")
```

*Recorded outputs on the package website were captured with `gpt-4.1`;
`gpt-6-luna` may answer slightly differently.*

## Compile a module

Start from the sentiment classifier in Tutorial 5, compiled offline with
`LabeledFewShot()`:

```{r compile-offline}
#| eval: true
sig <- signature(
  "review -> sentiment: enum('positive', 'negative', 'neutral')",
  instructions = "Classify the sentiment of this product review."
)

trainset <- tibble::tribble(
  ~review,            ~sentiment,
  "Love it!",         "positive",
  "Hate it!",         "negative",
  "It's okay.",       "neutral",
  "Amazing!",         "positive",
  "Terrible!",        "negative",
  "Meh.",             "neutral",
  "Best ever!",       "positive",
  "Worst purchase!",  "negative",
  "Fine I guess.",    "neutral"
)

classifier <- module(sig) |> compile(LabeledFewShot(k = 3L), trainset)
```

Verify that the compiled classifier runs:

```{r create-optimized}
#| cassette: true
run(classifier, review = "This product is fantastic!", .llm = chat)
```

## Save to a file

The simplest persistence path needs no extra packages: `save_program()` writes
a validated, versioned program artifact (signatures, demos, config, and
optimization state) to an `.rds` file, and `load_program()` rebuilds it in any
later session. `program_artifact_id()` returns its SHA-256 content identity:

```{r save-file}
#| eval: true
artifact_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_program(classifier, artifact_path)

loaded <- load_program(artifact_path)
identical(loaded$demos, classifier$demos)
identical(program_artifact_id(loaded), program_artifact_id(classifier))
```

The chat is intentionally not stored in the artifact—credentials never touch
disk—so pass `.llm` (or configure a default chat) when you run the restored
module:

```{r run-restored}
#| eval: false
run(loaded, review = "Worst product ever!", .llm = chat)
#> $sentiment
#> [1] "negative"
```

## Share versions with `pins`

When you want version history or shared team storage (such as S3, Google Cloud
Storage, or Posit Connect), `pin_module_config()` writes the same program
artifact to a `pins` board. The board below is a temporary folder that R
deletes when the session ends:

```{r save-config}
#| eval: !expr has_pins
board <- pins::board_temp()

pin_module_config(board, "sentiment-classifier", classifier)
```

For real use, pick a board that outlives the session:

```{r persistent-board}
#| eval: false
board <- pins::board_local()   # a folder in your user data directory
board <- pins::board_folder("pins") # or a folder in your project
```

Shared boards such as `pins::board_connect()`, `pins::board_s3()`, and
`pins::board_gcs()` work the same way. Each call to `pin_module_config()` with
the same name saves a new version: `pins::pin_versions(board, "sentiment-classifier")`
lists them, and `pins::pin_read(board, "sentiment-classifier", version = "<id>")`
reads an older one.

In a new session, connect to the same board, read the pin, and rebuild the
module:

```{r restore-config}
#| eval: !expr has_pins
config <- pins::pin_read(board, "sentiment-classifier")
restored <- restore_module_config(config)

identical(restored$demos, classifier$demos)
```

`restore_module_config()` and `load_program()` read the current artifact format
(version 6), so keep the code that compiled the module: if a future dsprrr
release updates the format, compile and save again. A module that holds R
functions or tools also needs a `registry` when you save and restore it; see
`?program_artifact`. For automated `targets` pipelines, Quarto reports, and
approval workflows, see [Run dsprrr in pipelines](orchestration.html).

## Save and inspect traces

A module records a trace for each call it makes, with token counts, latency,
cost, and model. Run the module a few times, then pin its traces next to the
configuration:

```{r save-traces}
#| cassette: true
run(classifier, review = "Great product!", .llm = chat)
run(classifier, review = "Not worth the money.", .llm = chat)
run(classifier, review = "Does the job.", .llm = chat)

if (has_pins) {
  pin_trace(board, "sentiment-traces", classifier)
}
```

`export_traces()` returns the same data as a tibble with one row per call,
including the call made right after compiling:

```{r analyze-traces}
export_traces(classifier)
```

The tibble leaves out prompts and responses by default, so you can share token
and latency logs without exposing user text. Pass `include_prompts = TRUE` or
`include_outputs = TRUE` (to `export_traces()` or `pin_trace()`) when you need
them. For a quick rollup of calls, tokens, and spend:

```{r summarize-traces}
summarize_traces(classifier)
```

## Where to go next

Across these six tutorials you have walked the full dsprrr loop: declare a
`signature()`, wrap it in `module()`, run it on vectors and data frames, score
it with `evaluate()`, improve it with `compile()` or `optimize_grid()`, and
save the result for reuse. From here:

- **Need reasoning, tools, or multi-step workflows?** Read
  [Choose a module type](advanced-modules.html) and
  [Chain modules into pipelines](chaining-modules.html).
- **Want stronger optimizers than grid search?** Read
  [Compile and optimize](compilation-optimization.html) and
  [Choose an optimizer](advanced-optimization.html).
- **Running dsprrr inside `targets` or Quarto?** Read
  [Run dsprrr in pipelines](orchestration.html).
